Hook.voiceover: You now know the laws. But knowing the rules does not tell a product manager on a Tuesday afternoon who must approve her new AI tool. A framework turns legal knowledge into daily decisions: who approves what, and at which stage.

Explain.voiceover: Welcome to module three, where we build your framework. As always, this course is educational and is not legal advice. Today's design is one practical example. Your organisation's size and legal position will change the details.

slide.title: Designing an AI Governance Framework
slide.body: Module 3 · Lesson 11 of 14. Footer line: Educational, not legal advice.

Explain.voiceover: A practical framework uses the six building blocks from lesson one, and gives each one an owner. Start with roles. The accountable executive is a senior leader who owns AI risk and approves high-risk uses. The AI governance group brings together legal, privacy, security, risk, technology and the business, to review new systems and set standards.

slide.title: Roles
slide.body: Org diagram: Accountable executive (top) → AI governance group (legal, privacy, security, risk, technology, business)

Explain.voiceover: The data protection officer advises on data protection, reviews DPIAs and monitors compliance, but does not own the business decision. And system owners are the business leaders responsible for each AI system, day to day.

slide.title: Roles
slide.body: Same diagram, adding: DPO (side box, dotted line: advises and monitors) · System owners (below: day-to-day responsibility)

Explain.voiceover: Next come a short list of principles, then an inventory where every system is recorded, classified and assessed, as we practised in modules one and two. Monitoring covers regular checks, incident handling and a yearly review.

slide.title: The other building blocks
slide.body: Principles: lawful · human oversight · fairness · transparency · privacy and security · accountability · Inventory, classification, assessment · Monitoring: checks, incidents, yearly review

Explain.voiceover: Lifecycle controls tie it together. The approval path follows the lifecycle: intake, classification, assessment, approval, launch, monitoring and retirement. Higher-risk systems pass more gates.

slide.title: Lifecycle gates
slide.body: Seven gates in a line: Intake → Classification → Assessment → Approval → Launch → Monitoring → Retirement. Caption: higher risk = more gates

Explain.voiceover: You do not need to design everything from nothing. Voluntary frameworks, such as an international management system standard for AI and a widely used AI risk management framework, can give structure. But neither is a legal requirement, and following them does not by itself prove compliance.

slide.title: Voluntary frameworks
slide.body: Left: Voluntary standards and frameworks, give structure, show good practice (names added after verification). Right: Legal requirements, EU AI Act, GDPR, NDPA. Caption: helpful, but not proof of compliance

Explain.voiceover: Think of flight procedures at an airport. Pilots, air traffic control, ground staff and safety inspectors each have a defined role, and every plane passes the same checks in the same order before take-off. Nobody invents the process for each flight.
Explain.stock_query: ground crew checking airplane before takeoff

Demonstrate.voiceover: From now on, your capstone uses one sample organisation: Velmora Tradeways Limited, a fictional logistics and trade-payments company. It has about six hundred staff, offices in Rotterdam and Lagos, and customers in both regions. It is a controller under the GDPR and the NDPA.
Velmora uses or plans six AI systems: a CV-screening tool bought from a vendor, a customer chatbot, a translation tool for staff, and a route-planning model built in-house.

slide.title: Velmora's AI systems
slide.body: 1. CV-screening tool (vendor, HR) · 2. Customer chatbot (website and app) · 3. Translation tool (staff) · 4. Route-planning model (in-house)

Demonstrate.voiceover: It also has an in-house credit-risk model that scores small business customers for payment terms, and a proposed driver-monitoring camera that detects signs of tiredness. Notice that these systems range from minimal risk to possibly high-risk.

slide.title: Velmora's AI systems
slide.body: 5. Credit-risk model (in-house, small business customers and sole traders) · 6. Driver-monitoring camera (proposed, tiredness detection)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Olumide Bankole, Velmora's new Head of Risk, designs the approval path. At intake, the system owner registers the idea in the AI inventory. Then the governance group classifies it under the AI Act, and checks whether personal data is involved.

slide.title: Velmora's approval path
slide.body: Gates 1 and 2 highlighted: Intake (system owner → AI inventory) → Classification (governance group: AI Act tier + personal data?)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Next comes a DPIA and, where needed, an AI Act assessment, reviewed by the data protection officer. Minimal-risk systems are approved by the governance group. High-risk systems also need the accountable executive. After launch, the system owner runs the agreed checks and reports to the group.

slide.title: Velmora's approval path
slide.body: Gates 3 to 5: Assessment (DPIA + AI Act assessment, DPO reviews) → Approval (minimal: governance group; high-risk: + accountable executive) → Launch and monitoring (system owner reports)

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to make the data protection officer the owner of every AI decision. That creates a conflict, because the officer must advise and check independently. Keep business ownership with system owners and the executive, and keep the officer in an advisory and monitoring role.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a practical framework has named roles, principles, an inventory, risk assessment, lifecycle controls and monitoring. Second, voluntary frameworks can give structure, but they are not legal requirements. Third, approval gates should match risk: higher-risk systems pass more gates and need more senior approval.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Named roles and six building blocks. 2. Voluntary frameworks help, but are not the law. 3. Gates and approval level match risk.

CTA.voiceover: In the exercise below this video, you will draw a one-page framework diagram for Velmora, showing who approves a new AI system and at which stage. Then test it by tracing the driver-monitoring camera through your diagram.

slide.title: Your exercise
slide.body: One-page framework diagram for Velmora · Roles and records at each stage · Two approval routes: minimal and high-risk · Trace the driver-monitoring camera · About 25 minutes

CTA.voiceover: Velmora is the centre of your capstone. In the next lesson, you start it by building an AI inventory and risk register. See you there.
